42855609.label: Objective
42855609.text: Herlyn-Werner-Wunderlich syndrome (HWWS) is a rare female reproductive tract malformation. Accurate preoperative diagnosis and classification are vital for surgical planning. This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic value of high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) T2-weighted MRI in the preoperative assessment and classification of HWWS.

42855609.label: Materials and methods
42855609.text: The study prospectively enrolled 84 patients clinically diagnosed with HWWS between May 2020 and January 2025. Seventy patients underwent pelvic MRI examinations, including high-resolution 3D T2 sequences (1 mm slice thickness) and conventional T2 TSE sequences, supplemented by large-field-of-view (FOV) T2 coronal imaging for urinary system evaluation and full-spine X-ray examinations for skeletal assessment. Two experienced radiologists independently evaluated the imaging features in a blinded manner, focusing on uterine morphology, obstruction sites, presence of communications, and related anomalies and complications. Consistency analysis was performed between imaging findings and surgical results in 52 surgical patients.

42855609.label: Results
42855609.text: Uterine morphology included: didelphys (54/70, 77.1%), complete septate (14/70, 20%), and bicornuate uterus (2/70, 2.9%). Among 52 surgical patients, 31 (59.6%) had vaginal-level obstruction with 18 (34.6%) Type I, 11 (21.2%) Type II, and 2 (3.8%) Type III, and 21 (40.4%) had cervical-level obstruction (Type IV and mixed). 3D T2 sequences identified 7 (63.6%) vaginal septum fistulas, outperforming TSE sequences, which detected none (0%) (p = 0.005). Associated findings were ipsilateral renal agenesis (98.6%), ovarian endometriosis (22.9%), hematosalpinx (22.9%), and spinal abnormalities (scoliosis (25.7%), mild scoliosis (41.4%).

42855609.label: Conclusion
42855609.text: High-resolution 3D T2 MRI is superior to conventional T2 TSE sequences in the preoperative evaluation of HWWS, especially for identifying communications and precisely locating obstruction sites.

42855609.label: Key points
42855609.text: Question Accurate preoperative structural assessment and classification of HWWS are clinically essential, yet conventional MRI has limitations in identifying fine anatomical structures and small communications. Findings High-resolution 3D T2 MRI outperforms conventional T2 TSE in identifying vaginal and cervical communications and precisely localizing obstruction sites in preoperative evaluation of HWWS. Critical relevance statement This study supports routine inclusion of 3D sequences in HWWS imaging protocols. Combined with renal and spinal assessment, it provides a comprehensive preoperative evaluation that enhances surgical planning precision and optimizes patient management strategies.

42878809.label: Objectives
42878809.text: Diagnostic workup of patients with acute cardiac symptoms, troponin elevation, and no acute myocardial infarction (AMI) criteria is challenging. Cardiac CT angiography (CCTA) rules out obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD). Adding late iodine enhancement and extracellular volume fraction (CCTA + LIE/ECV) provides insights into myocardial injury. However, the impact on working diagnosis, agreement with discharge diagnosis, and mid-term safety of implementing CCTA + LIE/ECV in the emergency department remains uncertain.

42878809.label: Materials and methods
42878809.text: Prospective study on consecutive patients presenting, from June 2018 to February 2025, with acute chest pain or equivalents, elevated troponin, and no AMI diagnosis, excluding previously revascularized patients. Patients underwent CCTA to rule out obstructive CAD (≥ 50% stenosis). CCTA-negative patients underwent myocardial tissue characterization with LIE; if negative, ECV was quantified.

42878809.label: Primary endpoint
42878809.text: modification of working diagnosis by CT. Secondary endpoints: agreement between CT and discharge diagnoses after standard-of-care assessment; mid-term major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) in CT-negative patients.

42878809.label: Results
42878809.text: Among 191 patients (age 70 [55-79] years; 53% men), CCTA identified obstructive CAD in 76/191 (40%). LIE/ECV were positive in 58/106 (55%) of CCTA-negative cases, revealing myocarditis in 32/106 (30%), AMI with non-obstructive CAD in 8/106 (8%), Takotsubo in 14/106 (13%), amyloidosis in 3/106 (3%), and dilated cardiomyopathy in 1/106 (1%). CT modified the working diagnosis in 91/191 (48%) patients. Agreement between CT and discharge diagnosis was 0.94 (95% CI 0.89-0.97). In patients with negative CCTA + LIE/ECV, no MACEs occurred after 24 [interquartile range, 19-29] months.

42878809.label: Conclusion
42878809.text: In patients with acute symptoms, elevated troponin, and no AMI, a protocol combining CCTA + LIE/ECV enables etiologic assessment of coronary and myocardial conditions, refines working diagnosis, and entails a favorable prognosis when negative.

42878809.label: Key points
42878809.text: Question Patients with acute cardiac symptoms, troponin elevation, and no evidence of acute myocardial infarction represent a diagnostic challenge: cardiac CT with late iodine enhancement may have diagnostic and prognostic implications. Findings CT angiography with late iodine enhancement provided a diagnosis in 75% of patients and modified the working diagnosis in 48%. In the 25% CT-negative patients, no adverse events occurred at mid-term follow-up. Clinical relevance A CT protocol including coronary artery evaluation and myocardial tissue characterization may provide a rapid etiological diagnosis in patients with acute symptoms and troponin elevation, potentially supporting earlier clinical decision-making and reducing the need for additional downstream testing.

42880959.text: Somatostatin receptor type 2 is highly expressed in meningiomas and can be quantified using [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET. The Krenning score, originally developed for [111In]In-octreotide scintigraphy, remains the standard visual grading system for somatostatin receptor expression and is widely used to guide eligibility for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy. However, visual grading may not optimally translate to intracranial disease. This study evaluated the relationship between brain-specific quantitative PET parameters-SUVmax and SUV ratio normalized to the superior sagittal sinus (SUVRsss)-and the Krenning score in meningioma. Methods: This single-institution retrospective study included 44 patients (70 meningiomas) who underwent clinical vertex-to-thigh [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT. Quantitative parameters (SUVmax, SUVRsss, lesion size) were extracted from coregistered PET and MR images. Spearman rank correlation analysis was performed to assess associations between imaging variables and Krenning score. Differences in quantitative PET parameters across Krenning categories were evaluated using Kruskal-Wallis test and Holm-Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney U test. Receiver-operating-characteristic curve analysis using the Youden J index identified optimal cutoffs for clinically relevant thresholds (Krenning score of <3 vs. ≥3 and 3 vs. 4). Results: SUVRsss and SUVmax were strongly correlated with the Krenning score (SUVRsss: Spearman ρ = 0.70; 95% CI, 0.55-0.82; SUVmax: Spearman ρ = 0.77; 95% CI, 0.64-0.85; P < 0.0001). PET parameters differed significantly across Krenning categories (all P < 0.001). SUVRsss optimal thresholds were 9.00 (area under the curve [AUC], 0.86; 95% CI, 0.74-0.96) for Krenning scores of 2 versus 3 and 29.84 (AUC, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.93-1.00) for Krenning scores of 3 versus 4. SUVmax optimal thresholds were 7.20 (AUC, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.84-0.99) and 30.70 (AUC, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.95-1.00), respectively. Conclusion: SUVRsss and SUVmax are complementary quantitative correlates of Krenning scores 2-4 in [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET-visible, MRI-measurable meningiomas. Brain-only PET evaluation may provide an alternative to liver- and spleen-based visual grading and reduce the need for whole-body imaging in selected settings. Receiver-operating-characteristic curve-derived SUV thresholds correspond to Krenning scores used for eligibility for treatment with peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, supporting further evaluation of quantitative PET parameters for theranostic decision-making for patients with meningioma.

42944909.label: Objective
42944909.text: Postoperative risk estimation in retroperitoneal liposarcoma (RPLS) remains challenging because conventional clinicopathologic models capture only part of its biological heterogeneity. We aimed to develop and externally evaluate a postoperative prognostic model integrating preoperative CT features with postoperative clinicopathologic information to estimate overall survival (OS) after RPLS resection.

42944909.label: Materials and methods
42944909.text: This bicentric retrospective study included 367 patients who underwent complete RPLS resection between 2009 and 2021. Institution 1 provided the training cohort (n = 128) and internal validation cohort (n = 55); Institution 2 provided the external test cohort (n = 184). A radiomics signature was constructed from three-dimensional tumor features. A deep-learning signature was derived from the largest axial tumor section using an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-101 trained with Cox partial-likelihood loss. Clinical variables underwent univariable and multivariable Cox regression analysis. The retained clinicopathologic variables and imaging signatures were integrated into a combined model termed RDCS.

42944909.label: Results
42944909.text: During follow-up, 71, 30, and 107 patients died in the training, internal validation, and external test cohorts, respectively. The corresponding RDCS C-indices were 0.775, 0.704, and 0.725, each higher than those of the individual radiomics, deep-learning, and clinical models. Calibration curves showed agreement between predicted and observed survival. Decision-curve analysis suggested potential clinical utility within the evaluated thresholds. In a separate exploratory comparison in the external primary-tumor subset (n = 82), C-indices were 0.746 for RDCS and 0.590 for the official Sarculator application.

42944909.label: Conclusion
42944909.text: RDCS estimates OS after complete RPLS resection using preoperative CT-derived imaging signatures and postoperative clinicopathologic information. RDCS may complement established postoperative prognostic tools, but its application in surveillance and clinical management requires prospective validation and clinical impact assessment.

42957209.text: Our purpose was to evaluate whether [18F]F-fluciclovine PET/CT detects sites of disease in patients with biochemical recurrence (BCR) of prostate cancer and negative findings on prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET and to assess its impact on intended management. Methods: In this prospective single-arm study, 50 patients with BCR (prostate-specific antigen [PSA] ≥ 0.2 ng/mL) and negative findings on PSMA PET underwent [18F]F-fluciclovine PET/CT within 30 d of the previous imaging. Detection rate, distribution of disease, PSA-stratified analysis, management impact, and correct localization rate were assessed using descriptive statistics and exact CI. Results: [18F]F-fluciclovine PET had positive findings in 28 of 50 patients (56%; 95% CI, 41%-70%). Disease was confined to the prostate bed in 14 patients (50%), whereas 14 (50%) demonstrated nodal or distant metastases. Detection rate increased with PSA, from 44% at a PSA of 0.2-0.5 ng/mL to 100% at a PSA of 5 ng/mL or higher. The intended management changed in 71% of patients after the [18F]F-fluciclovine PET: 87% of patients with positive findings and 54% with negative findings. Among patients with an available reference standard (n = 14), all positive findings were confirmed to be true-positive. Conclusion: [18F]F-fluciclovine PET detected recurrent disease in over half of patients with negative PSMA PET findings and frequently altered management, supporting its complementary role in selected patients with BCR.

42975709.text: While conventional ultrasonography (US) remains the first-line imaging modality for scrotal pathology, multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) has emerged as a valuable problem-solving tool for indeterminate US findings. Owing to its superior soft-tissue contrast, functional imaging capabilities, and operator independence, mpMRI allows for the precise localization and characterization of scrotal lesions. This paper from the European Society of Urogenital Radiology Scrotal and Penile Imaging Working Group provides a comprehensive, evidence-based overview of scrotal mpMRI for a general radiologist. It details optimized imaging protocols, recommending a standard sequence of T1-weighted, T2-weighted, diffusion-weighted, and subtracted dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging. The article highlights key clinical indications, including the characterization of intratesticular and paratesticular masses, local staging of testicular germ cell tumors, and differentiation between germ cell and sex cord-stromal neoplasms. This paper familiarizes radiologists with normal MRI appearances and MRI findings of common scrotal diseases. Evidence-based recommendations for reporting basic MRI examinations of the scrotum are also provided. The potential of advanced techniques, such as diffusion tensor imaging and proton MR spectroscopy, and the future integration of artificial intelligence and radiomics, are also discussed. We hope the implementation of these recommendations into radiological practice will enhance diagnostic confidence and promote standardized practice in scrotal MRI for radiologists. KEY POINTS: While conventional ultrasound is the first-line modality for scrotal pathology, it can yield inconclusive findings regarding complex mass characterization and local tumor staging. Multiparametric MRI combines anatomical and functional data to accurately characterize scrotal masses, localize impalpable, undescended testes, and provide precise local tumor staging. Scrotal multiparametric MRI serves as a valuable problem-solving tool that enhances diagnostic confidence in sonographically indeterminate cases, prevents unnecessary radical orchiectomies, supports testis-sparing surgery or active surveillance, and standardizes radiological reporting templates to optimize personalized patient management.

42998159.label: Objective
42998159.text: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT) for gastric cancer T staging compared with conventional energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT).

42998159.label: Materials and methods
42998159.text: Fifty-three patients with preoperative PCD-CT and 54 patients with preoperative EID-CT were retrospectively enrolled. Two radiologists independently assessed the visibility and T stages using all available sequences, including virtual monoenergetic images (VMIs) from PCD-CT at 40, 50, 60, and 70 kiloelectron volt (keV) levels. The lesion detectability and diagnostic accuracy of the two CT systems were analyzed and compared. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of gastric cancer lesions were also measured.

42998159.label: Results
42998159.text: Five lesions in the PCD-CT group and 12 lesions in the EID-CT group could not be confidently identified. For visible lesions, the overall T staging accuracies were 85.4% (95% CI: 72.8-92.8%) for Reader 1 and 83.3% (95% CI: 70.4-91.3%) for Reader 2 on PCD-CT, compared with 73.8% (95% CI: 58.9-84.7%) for Reader 1 and 78.6% (95% CI: 64.1-88.3%) for Reader 2 on EID-CT. The interobserver agreement for both CT systems was excellent, with weighted kappa values of 0.807 (95% CI: 0.693-0.921) for PCD-CT and 0.832 (95% CI: 0.720-0.943) for EID-CT. Quantitative analysis showed significantly higher SNR and CNR on PCD-CT than EID-CT (both p < 0.05).

42998159.label: Conclusion
42998159.text: PCD-CT demonstrated significantly higher quantitative image quality metrics (SNR and CNR) and numerically higher diagnostic performance than EID-CT in this exploratory retrospective comparison. The potential value of PCD-CT in gastric cancer T staging warrants further validation.

42998159.label: Key points
42998159.text: Question The diagnostic performance and potential value of PCD-CT in gastric cancer T staging are still unclear. Findings PCD-CT showed significantly higher quantitative image quality metrics (SNR and CNR) and numerically higher diagnostic performance than EID-CT in this exploratory comparison. Clinical relevance PCD-CT may offer potential value in gastric cancer T staging.
